title: Robust Priority Assignment for Fixed Priority Real-Time Systems

extraction.paper_name: Robust Priority Assignment for Fixed Priority Real-Time Systems
extraction.paper_description: This paper introduces and defines the concept of a 'robust' priority ordering for fixed priority real-time systems. It presents a Robust Priority Assignment (RPA) algorithm that finds this robust ordering, which is the most appropriate priority ordering for systems subject to variable amounts of additional interference (e.g., interrupts, OS overheads). The paper proves the optimality and robustness of the RPA algorithm and identifies conditions under which 'Deadline minus Jitter' monotonic priority ordering forms a robust partial or complete ordering, improving the efficiency of priority assignment algorithms.

formal_description.statement: A task tau_i is schedulable if its worst-case response time R_i is less than or equal to its relative deadline D_i.

variables.R_i: Worst-case response time of task i

informal_sketch.intuition: A task is considered 'schedulable' if it always completes its execution before its specified deadline. This is the fundamental condition for real-time systems.
steps: Calculate the worst-case response time (R_i) for a given task tau_i, considering all possible interference and blocking.
Compare R_i with the task's relative deadline (D_i).
If R_i is less than or equal to D_i, the task is schedulable.
key_insights: The worst-case response time calculation is central to determining schedulability.
This condition applies to individual tasks; a system is schedulable if all its tasks meet this condition.

formal_description.statement: For a given system model, a priority assignment policy P is referred to as optimal if there are no systems, compliant with the system model, that are schedulable using another priority assignment policy Q that are not also schedulable using policy P.

variables.system_model: A defined set of rules and constraints for a real-time system
variables.schedulable_system: A system where all tasks meet their deadlines

assumptions: The system complies with the given system_model.
formal_description.conclusion: Policy P can find a schedulable ordering whenever any other policy Q can.

informal_sketch.intuition: An optimal priority assignment policy is the 'best' possible in terms of finding a working schedule. If any other policy can make a system schedulable, the optimal policy can also make it schedulable.
steps: Consider a system that is schedulable using some arbitrary priority policy Q.
An optimal policy P must also be able to find a priority assignment for that same system such that it remains schedulable.
If P fails to find a schedulable ordering for a system that Q can schedule, then P is not optimal.
key_insights: Optimality is about existence: if a schedulable ordering exists, the optimal policy will find one.
It does not imply uniqueness or maximizing slack, only finding *a* feasible solution.

formal_description.statement: For a given system model and additional interference function E_i_w_alpha, a priority assignment policy P is referred to as robust if there are no systems, compliant with the system model, that are both schedulable and can tolerate additional interference characterized by a scaling factor alpha using another priority assignment policy Q that are not also both schedulable and can tolerate additional interference characterized by the same or larger scaling factor alpha_prime (where alpha_prime >= alpha) using priority assignment policy P.

variables.system_model: A defined set of rules and constraints for a real-time system
variables.E_i_w_alpha: Additional interference function for priority i, time interval w, and scaling factor alpha
variables.alpha_prime: Scaling factor for additional interference (alpha_prime >= alpha)
variables.schedulable_system: A system where all tasks meet their deadlines

assumptions: The system complies with the given system_model.
The additional interference function E_i_w_alpha is well-defined and monotonic.
formal_description.conclusion: Policy P can tolerate at least as much additional interference as any other policy Q, while maintaining schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: A robust priority assignment policy is the 'most resilient' to unexpected or variable interference. It ensures the system can handle the largest possible amount of additional interference compared to any other policy.
steps: Consider a system that is schedulable and can tolerate a certain level of additional interference (alpha) using policy Q.
A robust policy P must also be able to find a priority assignment for that same system such that it remains schedulable.
Furthermore, under policy P, the system must be able to tolerate an amount of interference (alpha_prime) that is at least as large as alpha (alpha_prime >= alpha).
key_insights: Robustness is about maximizing the system's tolerance to external disturbances.
It implies optimality in terms of schedulability, but adds the dimension of interference tolerance.
The comparison is based on the maximum scaling factor (alpha) of the interference function.

formal_description.statement: The Robust Priority Assignment (RPA) algorithm is an optimal priority assignment policy.
assumptions: The system model is 'analysable' (e.g., fixed priority, bounded execution times, periodic/sporadic tasks, SRP for resources, transactions, jitter, arbitrary deadlines).
Condition 1: The worst-case response time of a task is dependent on the set of higher priority tasks, but not on the relative priority ordering of those tasks.
Condition 2: The worst-case response time of a task may be dependent on the set of lower priority tasks, but not on the relative priority ordering of those tasks.
Condition 3: When the priorities of any two tasks are swapped, the worst-case response time of the task being assigned a higher priority cannot increase with respect to its previous value.
Condition 4: When the priorities of any two tasks are swapped, the worst-case response time of the task being assigned a lower priority cannot decrease with respect to its previous value.
formal_description.conclusion: The RPA algorithm will find a schedulable priority ordering if one exists for any system compliant with the assumptions.

informal_sketch.intuition: The RPA algorithm, by its design, is equivalent to Audsley's optimal priority assignment algorithm under specific conditions. Since Audsley's algorithm is known to be optimal, RPA inherits this property.
steps: The RPA algorithm iteratively assigns priorities from lowest to highest.
At each priority level, it selects an unassigned task that maximizes a certain metric (in RPA, it's the maximum tolerable additional interference).
The conditions (1-4) ensure that this greedy selection process does not 'paint itself into a corner' and can always find a schedulable assignment if one exists.
This behavior is analogous to Audsley's algorithm, which is proven optimal under these conditions.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def RPA_algorithm(task_set):
    assigned_tasks = []
    unassigned_tasks = list(task_set)
    priority_levels = len(task_set)

    for k in range(priority_levels, 0, -1): # Assign priorities from lowest (k=priority_levels) to highest (k=1)
        best_task_for_k = None
        max_tolerable_alpha = -1

        for tau_i in unassigned_tasks:
            # Temporarily assign tau_i to priority k, with assigned_tasks at higher priorities
            # Calculate max_alpha_i that tau_i can tolerate at priority k
            # (This involves a binary search for alpha_i for task tau_i at priority k)
            current_alpha_i = calculate_max_tolerable_alpha(tau_i, k, assigned_tasks, unassigned_tasks - {tau_i})

            if current_alpha_i is not None and current_alpha_i > max_tolerable_alpha:
                max_tolerable_alpha = current_alpha_i
                best_task_for_k = tau_i

        if best_task_for_k is None:
            return None # No schedulable ordering found

        assign_priority(best_task_for_k, k)
        assigned_tasks.append(best_task_for_k)
        unassigned_tasks.remove(best_task_for_k)

    return get_priority_ordering(assigned_tasks)
key_insights: The optimality stems from the algorithm's greedy, iterative assignment from lowest to highest priority.
The four conditions are crucial for ensuring that the local optimal choice at each step leads to a global optimal solution.
The proof relies on the established optimality of Audsley's algorithm.

formal_description.statement: The Robust Priority Assignment (RPA) algorithm is a robust priority assignment policy.

variables.P: Priority ordering found by RPA algorithm
variables.alpha_P_system: Maximum additional interference tolerated by system with ordering P
variables.alpha_Q_system: Maximum additional interference tolerated by system with ordering Q
variables.hep_k_P: Set of tasks with priority higher than or equal to k in P
variables.hp_k_P: Set of tasks with priority strictly higher than k in P
variables.lp_k_P: Set of tasks with priority strictly lower than k in P

assumptions: The system model and conditions from Theorem 1 apply.
The additional interference function E_i_w_alpha is monotonically non-decreasing in priority i and time interval w.
formal_description.conclusion: The RPA algorithm finds a priority ordering P such that alpha_P_system >= alpha_Q_system for any other ordering Q.

informal_sketch.intuition: The RPA algorithm is designed to maximize the system's tolerance to interference. The proof shows that any other priority ordering can be transformed into the RPA ordering without decreasing the overall system's interference tolerance.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that there exists an alternative priority ordering Q that tolerates *greater* additional interference than the ordering P found by RPA (i.e., alpha_Q_system > alpha_P_system).
Iteratively transform Q into P, starting from the lowest priority level (n down to 1).
At each iteration k, identify the task (tau_k) that RPA would assign to priority k.
If tau_k is not at priority k in the current ordering Q (but at a higher priority i), move tau_k from priority i to priority k, shifting tasks at priorities i+1 to k up one level.

Crucially, this transformation step is shown to *not decrease* the maximum additional interference the system can tolerate (alpha_Q_system_k >= alpha_Q_system_k-1). This is due to the properties of response time and interference functions (monotonicity, conditions 1-4).
After n such transformations, Q becomes P, and the accumulated result is alpha_P_system >= alpha_Q_system, which contradicts the initial assumption.
Therefore, RPA is robust.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def prove_RPA_is_robust(RPA_ordering_P, any_other_ordering_Q):
    # Assume alpha_Q_system > alpha_P_system for contradiction
    current_Q = deepcopy(any_other_ordering_Q)
    current_alpha_Q_system = calculate_system_alpha(current_Q)

    for k in range(len(task_set), 0, -1): # Iterate from lowest priority to highest
        task_at_P_k = get_task_at_priority(RPA_ordering_P, k)
        priority_of_task_at_P_k_in_current_Q = get_priority_of_task(current_Q, task_at_P_k)

        if priority_of_task_at_P_k_in_current_Q > k: # Task is at a higher priority in current_Q
            # Perform transformation: move task_at_P_k from its current higher priority to k
            # and shift intermediate tasks up.
            transformed_Q = perform_priority_swap_and_shift(current_Q, task_at_P_k, k)
            transformed_alpha_Q_system = calculate_system_alpha(transformed_Q)

            # Key step: prove transformed_alpha_Q_system >= current_alpha_Q_system
            # This relies on the properties of response time and interference (Conditions 1-4 and monotonicity)
            assert transformed_alpha_Q_system >= current_alpha_Q_system

            current_Q = transformed_Q
            current_alpha_Q_system = transformed_alpha_Q_system

    # After all transformations, current_Q is identical to RPA_ordering_P
    # So, alpha_P_system (which is current_alpha_Q_system) >= initial_alpha_Q_system
    # This contradicts the initial assumption (alpha_Q_system > alpha_P_system)
    return True # RPA is robust
key_insights: The proof uses an iterative transformation argument, a common technique in optimality proofs.
The monotonicity of the interference function and the response time properties (Conditions 1-4) are critical for ensuring that each transformation step does not reduce robustness.
The ability to transform any ordering into the RPA ordering without loss of robustness proves RPA's superiority in interference tolerance.

results.identifier: Theorem 3: D-JMPO Property for Mixed Systems

formal_description.statement: Given a mixed system, and two D-JM system model tasks, tau_A and tau_B, where tau_A has a larger value of deadline minus jitter than tau_B (D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B), then the additional interference characterized by alpha_A_i, tolerated by tau_A at an arbitrary priority i with tau_B at a higher priority, is at least as great as the additional interference alpha_B_i, tolerated by tau_B at priority i with tau_A at a higher priority.

variables.alpha_A_i: Max additional interference tolerated by tau_A at priority i (tau_B higher)
variables.alpha_B_i: Max additional interference tolerated by tau_B at priority i (tau_A higher)
variables.W_i: Busy period length for task at priority i
variables.C_X: Worst-case execution time of task X
variables.I_i_W_i_other_tasks: Interference from tasks other than tau_A and tau_B, and blocking, at priority i over interval W_i
variables.E_i_W_i_alpha: Additional interference function for priority i, interval W_i, and scaling factor alpha

assumptions: The system is a 'mixed system' (contains D-JM and non D-JM tasks).
tau_A and tau_B are D-JM system model tasks (pre-emptable, D <= T, no offsets).
The maximum interference on lower priority D-JM tasks caused by non D-JM tasks is monotonic in time interval and priority.
Tasks may make mutually exclusive access to shared resources according to SRP.
The interference term I_i_W_i_other_tasks (from other tasks and blocking) is the same irrespective of whether tau_A or tau_B is at priority i (assuming the other is higher priority).
formal_description.conclusion: alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i (tau_A, with larger D-J, is more robust at a given priority level).

informal_sketch.intuition: Tasks with a larger 'deadline minus jitter' value inherently have more 'slack' or flexibility. This theorem formalizes that this greater slack translates to a higher tolerance for additional interference when placed at the same priority level, assuming the other D-JM task is at a higher priority.
steps: Define the worst-case response time equation for a D-JM task tau_X at priority i, considering its own execution time (C_X), interference from other tasks and blocking (I_i_W_i_other_tasks), and additional interference (E_i_W_i_alpha). The busy period W_i is the smallest solution to: W_i = C_X + I_i_W_i_other_tasks + E_i_W_i_alpha.
A task tau_X is schedulable if its response time (W_i + J_X) is less than or equal to its deadline (D_X), which implies W_i <= D_X - J_X.
Let alpha_B_i be the maximum interference tau_B can tolerate at priority i (with tau_A higher). This means W_B_i + J_B <= D_B, or W_B_i <= D_B - J_B.
Given the condition D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B, it follows that D_A - J_A >= W_B_i. This implies that if tau_A had a busy period of W_B_i, it would be schedulable (W_B_i + J_A <= D_A).

Since the interference from other tasks (I_i_W_i_other_tasks) and blocking (B_i) are independent of whether tau_A or tau_B is at priority i, and the additional interference function E_i_W_i_alpha is monotonic, the task with greater slack (D_A - J_A) will be able to tolerate at least as much additional interference.
The proof concludes that alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i, meaning tau_A is more robust.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compare_robustness_D_JM_tasks(tau_A, tau_B, priority_i, other_tasks_interference_func, E_func):
    # Assume D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B

    # Calculate max alpha for tau_B at priority_i (with tau_A higher)
    # W_B_i is the busy period for tau_B
    alpha_B_i = find_max_alpha_for_task(
        task=tau_B, 
        priority=priority_i, 
        higher_priority_tasks_interference=other_tasks_interference_func, 
        E_func=E_func,
        deadline_constraint=tau_B.D - tau_B.J
    )

    # If tau_B is not schedulable even with 0 interference, alpha_B_i might be None or 0
    if alpha_B_i is None: 
        return True # If B can't tolerate anything, A can't tolerate less than nothing.

    # Now, check if tau_A can tolerate at least alpha_B_i at priority_i (with tau_B higher)
    # W_A_test is the busy period for tau_A if it tolerates alpha_B_i
    W_A_test = calculate_busy_period(
        task=tau_A, 
        priority=priority_i, 
        higher_priority_tasks_interference=other_tasks_interference_func, 
        E_func=E_func,
        alpha=alpha_B_i
    )

    # Check schedulability for tau_A with alpha_B_i
    is_A_schedulable_with_alpha_B_i = (W_A_test + tau_A.J <= tau_A.D)

    # The theorem states alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i. 
    # This implies that if tau_B is schedulable with alpha_B_i, then tau_A must also be schedulable with at least alpha_B_i.
    # The proof's logic is that D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B provides enough slack for tau_A.
    # The critical insight is that the 'other_tasks_interference_func' is the same in both scenarios.
    # The monotonicity of E_func ensures that if a smaller alpha works, a larger one might too.
    
    # The proof's final step 'W_B_i = W_A_i and alpha_B_i = alpha_A_i' is a simplification/typo.
    # The actual conclusion is that alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i due to the D-J slack and monotonicity.
    return is_A_schedulable_with_alpha_B_i # This implies alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i
key_insights: The 'Deadline minus Jitter' metric directly correlates with a task's inherent slack and thus its robustness to interference.
The independence of 'other task' interference and blocking from the specific D-JM task being analyzed at priority 'i' is crucial.
The monotonicity of the additional interference function ensures that if a certain level of interference is tolerated, any lower level is also tolerated.

results.identifier: Theorem 4: Robust Ordering for Mixed Systems with D-JMPO Partial Order

formal_description.statement: For a mixed system, where a schedulable priority ordering exists, there exists a robust priority ordering P with the D-JM system model tasks in 'Deadline minus Jitter' monotonic partial order.

variables.mixed_system: A system containing both D-JM and non D-JM tasks
variables.alpha_P_system: Maximum additional interference tolerated by system with ordering P
variables.alpha_Q_system: Maximum additional interference tolerated by system with ordering Q

assumptions: The system is a 'mixed system'.
A schedulable priority ordering exists for the system.
The conditions for Theorem 3 hold (especially D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B implies alpha_A_i >= alpha_B_i).
formal_description.conclusion: A robust priority ordering exists where D-JM tasks are ordered by D-JMPO relative to each other.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem extends the idea of D-JMPO optimality to mixed systems. It states that even when non D-JM tasks are present, the D-JM tasks should still be ordered among themselves according to their 'Deadline minus Jitter' values to achieve maximum robustness.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that there is an alternative priority ordering Q which tolerates greater additional interference than any ordering P that has D-JM tasks in D-JMPO.
Iteratively transform Q into an ordering P where D-JM tasks are in D-JMPO, without reducing the system's overall interference tolerance.
The transformation involves identifying two D-JM tasks, tau_A and tau_B, in Q that are out of D-JMPO order (i.e., tau_A has D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B, but tau_B is at a higher priority than tau_A).
Swap the priorities of tau_A and tau_B. This operation, based on Theorem 3, is guaranteed to not decrease the maximum additional interference the system can tolerate.
Repeat this process until all D-JM tasks are in D-JMPO relative to each other.
The resulting ordering P will have D-JM tasks in D-JMPO and will tolerate at least as much interference as the initial ordering Q, thus contradicting the initial assumption.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def prove_robust_ordering_has_D_JMPO_partial_order(mixed_system):
    # Assume for contradiction: exists Q such that alpha_Q_system > alpha_P_system 
    # where P is a D-JMPO partial order
    current_Q = get_initial_arbitrary_ordering(mixed_system)
    current_alpha_Q_system = calculate_system_alpha(current_Q)

    # Iterate until all D-JM tasks are in D-JMPO partial order
    while not is_D_JM_tasks_in_D_JMPO_partial_order(current_Q):
        # Find two D-JM tasks tau_A, tau_B in current_Q that are out of D-JMPO order
        # i.e., D_A - J_A >= D_B - J_B, but tau_B has higher priority than tau_A
        tau_A, tau_B = find_out_of_order_D_JM_tasks(current_Q)

        if tau_A is None: # No more out-of-order tasks, break
            break

        # Swap priorities of tau_A and tau_B
        transformed_Q = swap_priorities(current_Q, tau_A, tau_B)
        transformed_alpha_Q_system = calculate_system_alpha(transformed_Q)

        # By Theorem 3, this swap does not decrease robustness
        assert transformed_alpha_Q_system >= current_alpha_Q_system

        current_Q = transformed_Q
        current_alpha_Q_system = transformed_alpha_Q_system

    # The resulting current_Q is P (D-JMPO partial order)
    # And alpha_P_system (current_alpha_Q_system) >= initial_alpha_Q_system
    # This contradicts the initial assumption.
    return True # Such a robust ordering exists
key_insights: This theorem combines the robustness concept with the D-JMPO property.
It shows that the D-JMPO rule is not just optimal for specific system models but also robust within mixed systems.
The proof relies on Theorem 3 to justify that local swaps of D-JM tasks do not reduce overall system robustness.

dependencies: Theorem 3: D-JMPO Property for Mixed Systems

results.identifier: Theorem 5: RPA Generates D-JMPO Partial Order for Mixed Systems

formal_description.statement: For a mixed system, if a feasible priority ordering exists, then the RPA algorithm always generates a robust priority ordering with the D-JM system model tasks in 'Deadline minus Jitter' monotonic partial order, irrespective of the task execution times, and irrespective of the form of the additional interference function E_i_w_alpha (provided it meets monotonicity criteria).

variables.mixed_system: A system containing both D-JM and non D-JM tasks
variables.D_JM_system_model_tasks: Tasks compliant with the D-JM system model

assumptions: The system is a 'mixed system'.
A feasible priority ordering exists.
The additional interference function E_i_w_alpha is monotonically non-decreasing in priority i and time interval w.
The conditions for Theorem 1, 2, 3, and 4 hold.
formal_description.conclusion: The RPA algorithm naturally produces a robust ordering where D-JM tasks are ordered by D-JMPO among themselves.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is a powerful result: it states that the RPA algorithm, which is proven to find the most robust ordering, will *always* arrange the D-JM tasks according to their 'Deadline minus Jitter' values. This holds true regardless of specific task execution times or the exact nature of the interference, as long as the interference is monotonic.
steps: The RPA algorithm iteratively assigns priorities from lowest to highest.
At each priority level, it selects the unassigned task that can tolerate the most additional interference at that priority.
Theorem 3 proves that, among D-JM tasks, the one with the largest 'Deadline minus Jitter' value can tolerate at least as much additional interference as any other D-JM task at that priority level.

Therefore, when the RPA algorithm considers assigning a D-JM task to a priority level, it will naturally pick the D-JM task with the largest 'Deadline minus Jitter' value among the remaining unassigned D-JM tasks, because that task offers the highest robustness.
This greedy selection process, combined with Theorem 3, ensures that the D-JM tasks are assigned in D-JMPO relative to each other within the overall robust priority ordering.
This property holds irrespective of specific task parameters or the exact form of the monotonic interference function.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def RPA_generates_D_JMPO_partial_order(mixed_system):
    # RPA algorithm (as described in Theorem 1 sketch)
    # At each priority level k (from lowest to highest):
    #   candidate_tasks = unassigned_tasks
    #   best_task_for_k = None
    #   max_tolerable_alpha = -1

    #   for tau_i in candidate_tasks:
    #       alpha_i = calculate_max_tolerable_alpha(tau_i, k, ...)
    #       if alpha_i > max_tolerable_alpha:
    #           max_tolerable_alpha = alpha_i
    #           best_task_for_k = tau_i

    #   assign best_task_for_k to priority k

    # Key insight from Theorem 3:
    # If tau_i and tau_j are both D-JM tasks in candidate_tasks,
    # and (tau_i.D - tau_i.J) > (tau_j.D - tau_j.J),
    # then calculate_max_tolerable_alpha(tau_i, k, ...) >= calculate_max_tolerable_alpha(tau_j, k, ...).
    # Therefore, RPA will always prefer tau_i over tau_j if both are D-JM tasks and tau_i has larger D-J.
    # This ensures the D-JM tasks are ordered by D-JMPO.

    # The algorithm implicitly sorts D-JM tasks by D-J value when making selections.
    return True # RPA always generates D-JMPO partial order for D-JM tasks
key_insights: This theorem provides a strong guarantee about the structure of the robust priority ordering found by RPA.
It simplifies the search for robust orderings in mixed systems by confirming that D-JMPO is the correct relative ordering for D-JM tasks.
This insight leads to significant efficiency improvements for both RPA and Audsley's algorithm by reducing the number of tasks that need to be evaluated at each priority level.
